title: The Gang Makes Paddy's Great Again

jokes.text: When I first started working at Paddy's, this place was way more likely to host a dog fight than an event like tonight. In fact, when I first walked in, there were two dogs fighting. They were, like, strays or something that had wandered in? No one noticed.
jokes.setup: Dee is giving what sounds like a sincere, heartfelt speech about how much Paddy's has grown and evolved into a welcoming place.
jokes.punchline: The fond memory she chooses to contrast 'now' with is literal feral dogs fighting in the bar with zero staff awareness — immediately undermining the warm tone.
jokes.explanation: Solid cold open joke. The juxtaposition of a sincere speech with an absurdly specific and grim historical detail (stray dogs fighting, unnoticed) is very on-brand for the show. The 'no one noticed' tag lands as the actual punchline and earns an extra beat of laughter. Well-structured misdirection.

dialogue.line: when I first walked in, there were two dogs fighting. They were, like, strays or something that had wandered in? No one noticed.

jokes.text: Misunderstanding. Not racial.
jokes.setup: Dee mentions that the first time she met Frank, he pulled a gun on her, as an example of how far things have come.
jokes.punchline: Frank's only interjection is a terse, defensive clarification that it wasn't racial — which raises far more questions than it answers and implies it was still threatening regardless.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. The economy here is extraordinary — Frank doesn't deny pulling the gun, doesn't apologize, doesn't explain further. The clarification 'not racial' is so specific that it implies a full taxonomy of reasons Frank pulls guns on people, which is horrifying and hilarious. Perfect character integration: only Frank Reynolds would think this was the reassurance the room needed. Easily the strongest single-line joke in the cold open and a strong contender for the episode's best line.

dialogue.line: the first time I met Frank, he pulled a gun on me. Misunderstanding. Not racial.

jokes.text: Oh. You think those liberal morons bought it? Oh, yeah! They bought every word you said.
jokes.setup: Dee just gave an earnest-sounding speech about inclusivity and Paddy's welcoming nature, apparently to genuine applause.
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts immediately to the gang's true cynical motive — the whole speech was manufactured to manipulate liberal customers, fully reversing the warmth of the cold open.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny structural move: establish apparent sincerity, then immediately reveal the gang's true awful motive. The rewatch value is strong because on second viewing the phoniness of the speech is obvious. The 'liberal morons' line is the thesis statement of the episode's satirical engine. Competent but expected for this show.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You think those liberal morons bought it?

jokes.text: Conservative Whine — it's spelled with an 'H,' 'cause it's like 'We're whining.' It's a pun. It's a play on the word 'wine.' Yeah. Yeah, Mac, I get it. I came up with it.
jokes.setup: Mac is excitedly pointing out a wine label they created called 'Conservative Whine.'
jokes.punchline: Mac over-explains the pun in exhaustive detail to Charlie, who keeps shutting him down because he invented it — the joke being that Mac is mansplaining someone's own idea back to them while also being proud of a pretty weak pun.
jokes.explanation: Two-layered joke: the actual pun (Conservative Whine/Wine) plus the comedic dynamic of Mac over-explaining someone's own joke to them. The frustration of 'I came up with it' is relatable and plays well. Mac's obliviousness is on-brand. Competent comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: it's called 'Conservative Whine,' but it's spelled with an 'H,' 'cause it's like 'We're whining.' It's a pun. It's a play on the word 'wine.'

jokes.text: We're squeezing those liberal boners for all they got, and we're just gonna keep on squeezing them.
jokes.setup: The gang is celebrating their scheme to exploit liberal customers.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's chosen metaphor for financial exploitation is aggressively sexual and weirdly specific — 'liberal boners' creates an absurd image that derails the conversation.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's verbal weirdness is well-established but 'liberal boners' as a metaphor for monetization is a mid-tier Charlie non-sequitur. Gets a chuckle from its bluntness but isn't a particularly inspired moment.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It's all he ever makes and it's un-edible.

jokes.text: We're gonna make Paddy's great again.
jokes.setup: The gang is scheming about their next move to exploit a different crowd.
jokes.punchline: Charlie drops the Trump campaign slogan, implying the gang's plan is essentially a MAGA strategy applied to a dive bar — the joke being that this is the level of political sophistication these people operate at.
jokes.explanation: The slogan drop is the episode's title and central satirical conceit, so it lands with appropriate weight here. However, the joke is essentially the reference itself without much additional twist. Functional for establishing the episode's premise but not a creative high point.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mac reveals his muscular physique unprompted

jokes.text: Mac's Famous Mac and Cheese and some energy drinks for everybody. It's all he ever makes and it's un-edible.
jokes.setup: Mac proudly presents food he made for the planning meeting.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately and flatly labels it 'un-edible' as if this is simply a known fact of life — using the wrong word ('un-edible' instead of 'inedible') as a bonus Charlie malapropism.
jokes.explanation: 'Un-edible' is a lovely Charlie-ism — his malapropped vocabulary is a consistent character detail. The joke works on two levels: the insult itself and the linguistic error. Mac's obliviousness to the insult rounds it out. Solid mid-tier character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: He's fat, he's skinny, he's muscular, it's... It's best to ignore it.

jokes.text: No one ever really knows what's going on with Mac. He's fat, he's skinny, he's muscular, it's... It's best to ignore it. It's really a cry for help and attention, I think, so what you do in that situation is you ignore those. Yeah, treat it like a baby. Treat it like a toddler.
jokes.setup: Mac's physique reveal has been met with confusion and the group is trying to get back to business.
jokes.punchline: Dee and Charlie casually explain that Mac's physical transformations are a known recurring psychological crisis that the group has developed a child-rearing strategy to handle.
jokes.explanation: The 'treat it like a toddler' parenting advice applied to a grown man's desperate need for validation is a sharp character observation that doubles as meta-commentary on Mac's arc across the series. The escalation from 'ignore it' to actual childcare strategy is well-paced. Very quotable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You guys like me, right?

jokes.text: Why did I... why did I do it? Nobody knows. We don't know.
jokes.setup: Mac is being ignored and the group is moving on. He apparently got massively ripped with no plan for how it would help.
jokes.punchline: Mac sincerely asks why he did it; Charlie's response — 'Nobody knows' — is delivered with complete earnestness, as if it's a genuine mystery of the universe.
jokes.explanation: The collaborative bafflement between Mac and Charlie — with Charlie offering no comfort, just cosmic uncertainty — is a lovely little beat. It encapsulates Mac's season-long identity crisis in two lines. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Cindy
dialogue.line: Murphy's Pub? It's around the corner from you guys. Oh, the bar, the bar. The super successful bar around the corner.

jokes.text: The Waitress phone call interrupting the planning meeting — Charlie repeatedly stepping away mid-plan to take calls from his girlfriend.
jokes.setup: Cindy is in the middle of presenting an important plan. Charlie's phone rings.
jokes.punchline: Charlie takes the call from The Waitress and has a banal check-in conversation ('Is the TV just not working?'), completely derailing the meeting — revealing that his relationship has domesticated him in the most mundane way.
jokes.explanation: Charlie Day's obsessive love of The Waitress across the whole series makes it deeply ironic and funny that now that he finally has her, it's this boring domestic relationship. The TV check-in is perfectly mundane. Strong character integration — this joke only works for Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Hello? Yeah, hello? No, I can't talk right now, I'm in a very important business meeting. What? No, I don't know what you're talking about. I didn't do anything. Well, yeah, but that was different. No, you can't just come down here. I said you can't just come down here!

jokes.text: It has finally arrived... [crate opens to reveal Dennis sex doll] Is that a sex doll? Yeah. Is that Dennis?
jokes.setup: Mac excitedly announces that something has 'finally arrived' in a crate — after Frank guesses 'another rocket launcher,' the anticipation is built for something extraordinary.
jokes.punchline: It's a custom sex doll made to look like Dennis, their missing friend — which is both horrifying and immediately explained away by Mac with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout comedic moments. Frank's 'another rocket launcher' throwaway is itself a great joke (implying this has happened before), but the actual reveal tops it completely. A custom Dennis sex doll is a perfect encapsulation of Mac's desperate, repressed attachment to Dennis — it's character-driven absurdism at its best, and the season's driving comedic premise is established in a single visual. The 'another rocket launcher' detail rewards attentive viewers. Easily among the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: Another rocket launcher.
jokes.setup: Mac says something 'much cooler' than what Frank guessed arrived in the crate.
jokes.punchline: Frank's guess is 'another rocket launcher' — delivered flatly, implying this crate-delivery scenario has happened before and previously yielded a rocket launcher.
jokes.explanation: Three words of perfect Frank. The word 'another' does enormous work — it implies a whole history of rocket launcher deliveries to this bar that we never see. Frank's total nonchalance about owning rocket launchers is deeply in character and the economy is flawless. Comparable to the 'Not racial' joke in terms of doing maximum comedy with minimum words.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: you said I needed something Dennis-shaped to fill my hole

jokes.text: Because you told me to get one. Yeah, yeah, yeah. I was super sad about my old roommate leaving, and you said I needed something Dennis-shaped to fill my hole.
jokes.setup: Everyone demands to know why Mac got a Dennis sex doll.
jokes.punchline: Mac explains that Charlie told him he had 'a Dennis-shaped hole' to fill — which Mac interpreted literally as 'get a Dennis sex doll.' The double entendre of 'fill my hole' makes this even more loaded.
jokes.explanation: The 'Dennis-shaped hole in your life' metaphor being taken literally is excellent structure, and 'fill my hole' is a beautifully unintentional double entendre delivered with Mac's total sincerity. Mac's sexuality is a long-running theme of the show, so this lands with extra resonance for fans. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I obviously wanted you to, I don't know, maybe start dating or do something, not get a sex doll of your best friend.

jokes.text: No, Mac, I said that you obviously had a Dennis-shaped hole in your life that you needed to fill. How is that not the same thing?
jokes.setup: Mac has just explained his logic for getting a sex doll. Charlie tries to clarify what he actually meant.
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'How is that not the same thing?' — delivered with complete earnestness — reveals that he genuinely cannot distinguish between 'fill an emotional void' and 'purchase a sex doll of your friend.'
jokes.explanation: The callback to the previous joke with Mac's genuinely confused 'How is that not the same thing?' is a perfect extension. Mac's inability to see any distinction between emotional need and literal sex doll acquisition is played completely straight, which is funnier than any wink at the camera would be.

dialogue.line: He left him a contact number for where he was gonna be in North Dakota, but it ended up being a mental health line.

jokes.text: He left him a contact number for where he was gonna be in North Dakota, but it ended up being a mental health line. He miswrote one of the digits, and that... Nah, he knew what he was doing. He was avoiding him.
jokes.setup: Someone tries to put a charitable spin on the fact that Dennis left Mac a wrong contact number.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately cuts off the charitable explanation: 'Nah, he knew what he was doing. He was avoiding him.' Dennis deliberately gave Mac a mental health hotline number instead of his real number.
jokes.explanation: Dark and funny in the best Always Sunny way. Dennis replacing his real number with a mental health hotline for Mac — and the accidental aptness of that (Mac probably does need a mental health line) — is cruel but perfectly calibrated to Dennis's character. Frank's blunt truth-telling is spot-on character work.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's not like I'm gonna have sex with it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He's gonna have sex with that the second we walk out of this door.

jokes.text: It's not like I'm gonna have sex with it. He's gonna have sex with that the second we walk out of this door.
jokes.setup: Mac defensively insists the Dennis doll is just for 'companionship.'
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately delivers the obvious truth — he will absolutely have sex with it — as a flat, matter-of-fact aside, as if everyone in the room knows this.
jokes.explanation: A reliable comedic structure — character denies something obvious, another character states the obvious truth. Functional but doesn't reach beyond the formula.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He is. The second we leave, he's gonna bang it.

jokes.text: It might just be cool to have around for, like, companionship, you know? Nah, he wants to bang it. I'm not gonna bang it.
jokes.setup: Mac continues to insist the doll is just for companionship.
jokes.punchline: Frank again immediately cuts through it. The repeated denial/assertion structure escalates the joke each time.
jokes.explanation: Second iteration of the running gag — slightly diminishing returns from id 18, though Frank's escalating certainty is still funny. The gag is being milked here.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You want me to go find one?

jokes.text: Mac arrives shirtless in a duster with the Dennis sex doll.
jokes.setup: Everyone assumed Mac went to retrieve the doll to get rid of it and that he'd show up normally to Cindy's meeting.
jokes.punchline: Mac arrives shirtless in a western duster coat, still displaying his physique, still accompanied by the Dennis sex doll he was explicitly told to discard.
jokes.explanation: The shirtless duster is a perfect visual escalation of Mac's earlier failed 'unveiling' — he's doubling down on a strategy that wasn't working, now with added western flair. The fact that he brought the doll back despite being told to get rid of it is excellent character consistency. Two running threads converging in one image.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I cannot return the doll due to the custom nature of the usage of the doll

jokes.text: I tried, but apparently I cannot return the doll due to the custom nature of the usage of the doll.
jokes.setup: Mac was supposed to get rid of the Dennis sex doll.
jokes.punchline: He explains that the doll can't be returned due to 'the custom nature of the usage' — an absurdly bureaucratic euphemism for 'I had sex with it.'
jokes.explanation: The euphemism 'custom nature of the usage' is a beautifully constructed piece of Mac-speak — formal, evasive, and revealing all at once. It confirms what everyone predicted (Dee's 'he's gonna bang it') while adding the comedic bonus of Mac having apparently tried to return it to a store. The logistics implied are extremely funny.

dialogue.line: Mac shirtless in a duster trying to incorporate it into the plan

jokes.text: About what? I'm shirtless in the duster. Oh, yeah. Why? Well, I thought that could work. Toward what? I don't know.
jokes.setup: Mac wants feedback on his shirtless duster look as a potential contribution to the plan.
jokes.punchline: He cannot articulate any reason why being shirtless would help the plan. 'I don't know' is his genuine final answer.
jokes.explanation: Mac's complete inability to articulate the value proposition of his own body is a continuation of the physique joke. The rapid-fire question-and-answer structure works well rhythmically.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You're not Dennis! You're never gonna be, all right?

jokes.text: Stop trying to shoehorn your shirtless-ness into plans that have no need for it.
jokes.setup: Mac keeps trying to insert himself into the plan based solely on his physique.
jokes.punchline: Cindy articulates the exact problem with Mac's approach using the word 'shoehorn' — which is both accurate and funny as an unexpected precise vocabulary choice for this situation.
jokes.explanation: 'Shoehorn your shirtless-ness' is a great line — alliterative, specific, and cutting. Cindy's sharp, no-nonsense character voice is well-established through lines like this. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I was picturing what Dennis might've said in the situation and Dennis just said something really funny.

jokes.text: I feel like this is what Dennis would've done. Yeah, but Dennis had a reason for it, man! And you're not Dennis! You're never gonna be, all right? So just drop it.
jokes.setup: Mac tries to justify his shirtlessness by saying it's what Dennis would do.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's correction — 'Dennis had a reason for it' and 'You're not Dennis' — implies that Dennis's physique-as-plan-asset was legitimate (he used it to manipulate people) while Mac is just... flexing with no agenda.
jokes.explanation: This joke is richer for long-time viewers who remember Dennis's calculated use of his appearance as a tool for manipulation. The implication that Dennis's narcissism was at least weaponized while Mac's is just... narcissism, is a sharp character distinction.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It called me a bird.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yes!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It did.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Exactly.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We all heard it.

jokes.text: Oh, something the doll just said. What? Nice one, man. The doll talks to you now?
jokes.setup: Mac is apparently picturing what Dennis would say in various situations.
jokes.punchline: Frank and Mac both appear to be responding to remarks 'from the doll' — reacting to it as if it said something funny — while Dee escalates to asking if the doll talks to Mac now.
jokes.explanation: The gradual escalation of the group treating the Dennis doll as a present, opinionated entity is a strong running thread. The absurdist leap from 'I'm imagining what Dennis would say' to 'the doll talks' happens naturally through the group's shared psychosis. Good escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I requested that the doll feel as though it's in mid-conversation.

jokes.text: It was about you, Dee. It called me a bird. Yes! It did. So you did hear it. We all heard it. Bird. How is that funny? It's-it's really not. It's just the way Dennis would have said it.
jokes.setup: The doll apparently said something funny, and Mac says it was about Dee.
jokes.punchline: The 'joke' the doll made was just calling Dee a 'bird' — which is not inherently funny, but the entire group agrees they can picture Dennis saying it in a way that makes it hilarious. The meta-joke is about the ineffable quality of delivery.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's smartest jokes. 'Bird' — the gang's nickname for Dee — is objectively not a clever insult, but the joke is about how Dennis's particular delivery makes it land. This is simultaneously a callback to years of Dee being called a bird, a character tribute to Glenn Howerton's performance, AND a meta-comment on how comedy is about delivery not content. The group's unanimous 'we all heard it' despite the doll being inanimate adds the right absurdist layer. 'How is that funny? It's-it's really not. It's just the way Dennis would have said it.' is a genuinely insightful line about comedy itself.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: using all the glitter and stuff was a great idea... maybe you would slather it all over my naked torso

jokes.text: The blowjob mouth — did it come standard on the doll or did you customize that? It's not a blowjob mouth, Dee. Don't be crass. I requested that the doll feel as though it's in mid-conversation.
jokes.setup: Cindy asks for questions about the plan. Dee's hand goes up.
jokes.punchline: Dee asks if the doll's mouth came standard — Mac indignantly corrects her: he requested it be 'in mid-conversation.' The euphemism is simultaneously more absurd and more revealing than just admitting what it is.
jokes.explanation: 'I requested that the doll feel as though it's in mid-conversation' is an outstanding euphemism — both a brilliant way to avoid admitting what it actually is AND accidentally a window into Mac's deeper longing for actual conversation with Dennis. It's funny and strangely poignant. Highly quotable. Mac's indignation at the word 'blowjob' while making zero attempt to explain what 'mid-conversation' actually means is perfect character work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I know it's just a lifeless thing that Mac pumps his loads into, but it's in my head.

jokes.text: Not about the sex doll.
jokes.setup: Cindy asks for other questions after answering the blowjob mouth inquiry.
jokes.punchline: Before anyone can speak, she preemptively rules out the doll as a topic.
jokes.explanation: Three words, great rhythm. Cindy's preemptive exclusion implies she's already learned this lesson the hard way. Perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: that's bleach. I cleaned him.

dialogue.speaker: Gang
dialogue.line: Well, then why did you clean it?

jokes.text: 'Liberal Tears' — it's so funny because the liberals are always whining about stuff and the conservatives drink it up. They're drinking their tears.
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining the second wine label concept to Charlie.
jokes.punchline: Mac explains the double meaning of 'Liberal Tears' with zero irony — not noticing that his explanation of why it's funny is itself a demonstration of exactly the kind of smugly self-satisfied conservative 'owning the libs' mentality the show is satirizing.
jokes.explanation: The joke is mild — it's satirizing a specific brand of political smugness by having Mac perform it earnestly. Functional but not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It doesn't like what I'm wearing and it thinks I need more makeup.

jokes.text: I was thinking maybe you would slather it all over my naked torso and we would use that. Why? Well, that can just be a part of the plan, you know? It doesn't have anything to do with anything, though. Well, then why did I do all this working out, Charlie?
jokes.setup: Cindy mentions glitter as part of the plan. Mac sees an opening.
jokes.punchline: Mac pivots to suggesting he get glitter slathered on his naked torso for the plan — Charlie points out this has nothing to do with anything — Mac's devastated 'Well, then why did I do all this working out?' reveals the whole fitness journey was purely for display purposes with no actual plan.
jokes.explanation: 'Well, then why did I do all this working out?' is the comedic thesis of the Mac physique subplot — he got massively ripped and has absolutely no plan for what to do with it. The existential plaintiveness of this question, combined with the behind-the-scenes knowledge that Rob McElhenney actually trained for a year for this, gives the joke a beautiful extra layer.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Dennis, does Mac look fat?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah.

jokes.text: Dee in a blonde wig and flattering outfit — 'Wow, Dee, you look great! Really? Yeah, I hate to admit it, but this look's kind of working for you.'
jokes.setup: Dee has gotten done up to flirt with the security guard. The gang sees her.
jokes.punchline: The gang is genuinely surprised she looks good — 'I hate to admit it' implies it's against their preferences to acknowledge Dee as attractive. The 'working for you' as a backhanded compliment suggests normally she doesn't.
jokes.explanation: A reliable Always Sunny joke type — the gang reluctantly acknowledging Dee has worth. The 'I hate to admit it' is good, but the joke is fairly formulaic within the show's established patterns.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: it also thinks Mac looks fat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's... that's a lie!

jokes.text: Look, I know it's just a lifeless thing that Mac pumps his loads into, but it's in my head.
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to stay in character to flirt with the guard but is distracted by the Dennis doll.
jokes.punchline: Her way of describing the doll — 'a lifeless thing that Mac pumps his loads into' — while also admitting it's affecting her psychologically is perfectly absurd. She can't look away from the doll despite understanding exactly what it is.
jokes.explanation: Dee naming the thing for what it is so bluntly while in the middle of a seduction is very funny. The confirmed 'pumps his loads into' is satisfying payoff to the earlier running gag about whether Mac was having sex with it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: what do you care if Dennis is back?

jokes.text: No, that's bleach. I cleaned him. Well, then why did you clean it? Why did you clean it?
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee insist they can smell something on the doll. Mac says it's bleach.
jokes.punchline: The question 'Why did you clean it?' — with the implication that cleaning implies use — hits Mac like an accusation. The simultaneous 'Why did you clean it?' from multiple people is a perfect comedic beat.
jokes.explanation: The trap of Mac's own explanation — the fact that cleaning implies prior use — is well-constructed. The simultaneous 'why did you clean it' from Frank and Dee landing as a united accusation is good timing. Solid payoff to the doll running gag.

dialogue.speaker: The Waitress
dialogue.line: it's like Dennis is sitting in our apartment just staring at us.

jokes.text: It's in my head, too. How? It doesn't like what I'm wearing and it thinks I need more makeup.
jokes.setup: Dee admitted the doll is in her head. Someone asks how.
jokes.punchline: Dee is hearing criticism from the inanimate Dennis doll about her outfit and makeup — and she's taking it seriously.
jokes.explanation: Dee being so conditioned by Dennis's fashion criticism that she's now hallucinating it from his effigy is a great character joke. The specificity ('needs more makeup') makes it land — it's exactly what Dennis would say. Good character integration: this only works because of the established Dennis/Dee dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: The Waitress
dialogue.line: You talk to the doll, and-and not me so much.

jokes.text: It also thinks Mac looks fat. That's... that's a lie! I know, I know, but it... that's just what he thinks. Let me ask it. Dennis, does Mac look fat?
jokes.setup: The gang is now fully engaging with the Dennis doll as if it has opinions.
jokes.punchline: Mac's indignant denial, then Mac turning to the doll to ask it directly if he looks fat — treating a sex doll as an authority on his physique — after spending the episode desperately displaying said physique.
jokes.explanation: Perfect convergence of two running threads: Mac's physique insecurity and the doll-as-Dennis dynamic. Mac worked out for a year, refuses to wear a shirt, and is now desperately seeking validation from a sex doll. The fact that he asks the doll directly — 'Dennis, does Mac look fat?' — is a lovely absurdist culmination.

dialogue.line: those just say 'wine.'

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We thought 'Liberal Tears' was maybe gonna be confusing

jokes.text: It doesn't like the labels on the... these are dumb 'Liberal Tears,' right. Does it say 'tear' or does it say 'tear'? It's confusing.
jokes.setup: The Dennis doll has apparently weighed in on the wine labels.
jokes.punchline: Charlie, now fully on board with the doll's opinions, raises the 'tear/tear' homophone issue — which was already a concern earlier — and attributes it to the doll's critique.
jokes.explanation: The homophone joke ('tear' as in crying vs. 'tear' as in ripping) is moderately funny but the execution here is somewhat muddled. The doll connection is a running gag extension that works but doesn't add much.

dialogue.speaker: The Waitress
dialogue.line: Oh, I fucked him.

jokes.text: So it's called 'Liberal Tears.' I don't know if it's confusing, that's not really the point. What I want to know is what do you think of this? I think it's super weird. Like in a good way or like...? Like in the creepiest possible way, Charlie.
jokes.setup: Charlie is now at home showing The Waitress the Dennis sex doll.
jokes.punchline: He shows her the doll expecting approval; she delivers the clearest possible verdict — 'like in the creepiest possible way' — which Charlie processes not as a dealbreaker but as a nuance question.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's 'like in a good way or like...?' is a good beat — his genuine hope that this might somehow be a compliment reveals his total inability to read the room. The Waitress's clarity is a good straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: The Waitress
dialogue.line: it told me to drink this bottle of wine. And then it talked me into having sex with it.

jokes.text: It's kind of like Dennis is sitting in our apartment just staring at us. I know, but, like, look, you need someone to talk to, right? And I-I just, I can't be that guy right now. I'm so busy being a success and stuff. I'm sorry. You want me to talk to the doll?
jokes.setup: The Waitress is creeped out by the Dennis doll.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's solution to The Waitress needing emotional support is to suggest she talk to the Dennis sex doll — because Charlie is 'too busy being a success' (which is itself absurd given who Charlie is).
jokes.explanation: 'I'm so busy being a success and stuff' from Charlie Kelly — a man who famously can barely read — is a great character-specific absurdism. His pivot to assigning his girlfriend the sex doll as a therapist is perfectly deranged Charlie logic. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You're cheating on me. With Dennis!

jokes.text: It's already shamed Mac, which was pretty funny.
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to sell The Waitress on talking to the Dennis doll as a therapeutic option.
jokes.punchline: His selling point is that the doll already successfully shamed Mac — the callback to the crunches sequence — presented as a feature, not a bug.
jokes.explanation: Light meta-callback — Charlie remembering the Mac shaming as a positive testimonial for the doll's effectiveness is a funny character beat. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: The Waitress
dialogue.line: His voice is funny. It's-it's so high.

jokes.text: I fucked him. ♪ Bring me a higher love ♪
jokes.setup: Charlie calls home to tell The Waitress to get rid of the Dennis doll. He finds the apartment transformed in some way and asks 'What the hell is this?'
jokes.punchline: The Waitress simply admits: 'Oh, I fucked him.' The song 'Bring Me a Higher Love' plays immediately after — the music cue elevating the confession to absurd melodrama.
jokes.explanation: The best single punchline in the episode. 'Oh, I fucked him' is the perfect payoff to multiple converging threads: the running gag about who will inevitably have sex with the doll, Charlie assigning The Waitress to talk to it, and the doll-as-Dennis dynamic. The casualness of the confession, the simplicity of the three words, and the immediate musical sting of 'Bring Me a Higher Love' make this an exceptional comedic construction. It's the rare joke that gets funnier on rewatch because you can see it building from the moment the doll arrives. Comparable to the high-quality anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: You're cheating on me. With a doll. With Dennis!

jokes.text: Oh, it's just a-a new lighting setup. It-it washes me out. It's-it's a better look.
jokes.setup: Cindy notices something strange about Dee's setup
jokes.punchline: Dee has rearranged the lighting to suit the doll's critique of her appearance — she's decorating around it
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation callback. Dee has actually changed her environment based on the doll's fashion critique. She's now doing beauty lighting at a business operation because Dennis (via doll) told her to. The doll's influence is spreading and corrupting everything.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Do you have any more bottles of wine?

jokes.text: Well, yeah, I can see that. Why?! Um, because that's what it was designed for? You were... you were supposed to talk to it, not have sex with it! Okay, well, I did talk to it. And it told me to drink this bottle of wine. And then it talked me into having sex with it.
jokes.setup: Charlie is horrified that The Waitress had sex with the Dennis doll.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress's explanation: she talked to the doll, it told her to drink wine, and then it talked her into sex — delivered as a completely reasonable sequence of events, as if the doll is an autonomous agent.
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdism of 'it told me to drink wine... then it talked me into sex' extends the doll-as-real-entity gag to its logical extreme. The Waitress treating this as a reasonable chain of events is perfect deadpan. The structure is excellent — each step of her explanation is more absurd than the last.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm gonna break up with you!

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: I already said it.

jokes.text: Wait a second. This doesn't have anything to do with the doll, does it? Come on. Why would the doll...? No. The doll? What do we care about the doll? No?
jokes.setup: Cindy surveys the chaos: wrong labels, Dee's lighting, Frank's paralysis
jokes.punchline: Everyone denies the doll's involvement with hilariously unconvincing evasion
jokes.explanation: The collective denial is funny because we've seen all the doll's influence. The overlapping, poorly coordinated 'What do we care about the doll?' protests are textbook cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I think maybe some fresh titty will cheer you up, huh?

jokes.text: I can't... You know, this is cheating, by the way. You're cheating on me. Uh, with a doll. With Dennis!
jokes.setup: Charlie processes The Waitress having sex with the Dennis doll.
jokes.punchline: He upgrades his accusation from 'cheating with a doll' to 'cheating with Dennis' — treating it as an actual betrayal involving his actual absent friend.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'with a doll' to 'with Dennis' is a great escalation. Charlie fully subscribing to the doll-as-Dennis reality is funny, and the irony of Charlie being jealous of Dennis even while Dennis is literally a sex doll is well-layered.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dennis is gone, and he is not coming back. We have to accept that.

jokes.text: I can't... You know, this is cheating, by the way. You're cheating on me. Uh, with a doll. With Dennis!
jokes.setup: The Waitress has sex with the Dennis doll
jokes.punchline: Charlie's moral outrage that she cheated 'with Dennis' specifically — the specific betrayal is with his doll-friend
jokes.explanation: The 'with a doll' vs. 'with Dennis!' exchange is perfectly constructed. The Waitress's correction is absurd but Charlie insisting on the Dennis specificity is funnier. He's not upset about the doll, he's upset about Dennis. This touches on Charlie's always-simmering Dennis jealousy.

dialogue.line: She's kind of like Dennis but only way better. Better than Dennis.

jokes.text: His voice is funny. Oh, oh, oh! Go to hell! I hadn't noticed it. Go... You go right to hell! It's-it's so high.
jokes.setup: In the middle of the breakup confrontation, Mac notices something about Charlie's voice.
jokes.punchline: Mac points out that Charlie's voice is 'so high' — apparently for the first time — while Charlie is in the middle of a devastating emotional moment. Dee's 'Go to hell' response while Mac continues to analyze the voice is a perfect comedic collision.
jokes.explanation: The comedic collision of Mac analyzing Charlie's voice pitch during a breakup scene is good tonal whiplash. The specificity of 'his voice is funny' and 'it's so high' — said with genuine interest rather than cruelty — is characteristically Mac. Good disruption of the emotional scene.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I was playing his asshole.

jokes.text: Charlie, I'm breaking up with you. You're-you're breaking up with me? I'm gonna break up with you! I already said it. We think you should get out.
jokes.setup: The Waitress is breaking up with Charlie.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress uses 'we' — meaning herself and the Dennis doll — to tell Charlie to leave. She's broken up with Charlie on behalf of herself and the sex doll she just slept with.
jokes.explanation: 'We think you should get out' — The Waitress speaking on behalf of herself and the Dennis sex doll — is a great line. The implication that the doll is now an equal partner in the relationship and they're united against Charlie is perfectly absurd. The escalation from 'I'm breaking up with you' to 'we' is well-structured.

jokes.text: Wait, wait, wait. Okay. Do you have any more bottles of wine?
jokes.setup: Charlie has just been dumped and told to leave by his girlfriend and her new sex-doll partner.
jokes.punchline: His parting request is for wine — practical, undignified, and completely Charlie.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's coping mechanism being an immediate pivot to practical resource acquisition is very true to his character. The bathos of this small request after a major emotional moment is well-calibrated. Good economy.

dialogue.line: That's dead-on. Yeah, you nailed it.

jokes.text: I think maybe some fresh titty will cheer you up, huh?
jokes.setup: The gang is commiserating with Charlie at a strip club after his breakup.
jokes.punchline: Frank's attempt at emotional support is suggesting 'fresh titty' as the therapeutic solution — not from cruelty but from genuine belief this is helpful.
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank — his emotional intelligence running through the lens of his id. 'Fresh titty' as emotional first aid is very Frank. The delivery presumably makes this land harder than it reads.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't like it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Why do you have it?
It's for Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, Mac's shooting his loads into it?

jokes.text: I'm just pissed that Dennis did that to me. Dennis is a bastard, man. Right? Always has been, always has been.
jokes.setup: Charlie is processing being cheated on — with a Dennis sex doll.
jokes.punchline: The gang commiserates by blaming Dennis for the betrayal — as if Dennis himself cheated with The Waitress, not a rubber effigy. Mac's 'always has been, always has been' is delivered with real conviction about Dennis's historic perfidy.
jokes.explanation: The gang treating a sex doll's actions as Dennis's actual behavior is a funny extension of the episode's running absurdism. 'Dennis is a bastard, man. Always has been' as genuine betrayal is well-calibrated to the established dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You dress like it's 1998. Your look is played out and so are you. You're basic.

jokes.text: She's kind of like Dennis but only way better. Yeah. Yeah, yeah. Better than Dennis. I absolutely prefer her to Dennis. Right? I like her more.
jokes.setup: The gang is talking themselves into liking Cindy and moving on from Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Their praise of Cindy is entirely relational to Dennis — they like her because she's 'like Dennis but better' — revealing they haven't actually moved past Dennis; they're just transferring their Dennis dependency.
jokes.explanation: The punchline is embedded in the structure: every compliment for Cindy is actually about Dennis. The gang can't even praise someone without it being a Dennis comparison. Character-specific and thematically resonant.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You dress like it's 1998. Your look is played out and so are you. You're basic.

jokes.text: All right, what do we do with him? Not sure yet. But, uh, what do you say we do, like, three rounds of shots and figure it out after that?
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to figure out what to do with the Dennis sex doll.
jokes.punchline: Frank's solution to a complex problem involving a Dennis sex doll is 'three rounds of shots first.' The implication being that this is their standard decision-making process.
jokes.explanation: Functional gang character moment. Frank's 'shots first' approach to problem-solving is well-established. Reliable but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Cindy
dialogue.line: They're just gonna go back to treating you like shit the minute I leave!

jokes.text: Oh, God. Oh, yuck! No, stop! Stop it! Stop! Charlie, stop! How is this moving things forward? What are you doing? Oh, I was playing his asshole.
jokes.setup: The gang arrives to implement Cindy's plan at Murphy's Pub. Something unexpected is happening outside — Cindy reacts with horror.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, I was playing his asshole' — Charlie has apparently been playing the Dennis doll's anal opening like a wind instrument (or tuba mouthpiece) in public, as his contribution to the plan.
jokes.explanation: 'I was playing his asshole' is the single most quotable line in the episode and a strong contender for the most purely disgusting/funny Always Sunny revelation of the season opener. The misdirection is perfect — Cindy's physical revulsion sets up the reveal, and 'playing his asshole' as a deadpan explanation for a tuba-substitute is genuinely inspired. The convergence of the tuba plan + the Dennis doll in the most grotesque possible way is exceptional escalation. This is exactly the kind of joke Always Sunny does better than any other show on television.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I kind of like being the only woman. 'Cause it makes me feel special.

jokes.text: That part I got. Why?
jokes.setup: Charlie explains he was 'playing his asshole'
jokes.punchline: Cindy's response isn't disbelief that it happened, just a simple 'why' — she accepts the fact, only wants the rationale
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfect economy. 'That part I got' is the funniest way to establish that this is so normal for the gang that the act itself requires no explanation — only the motivation does. Cindy as the analytical outsider works beautifully here.

dialogue.line: You already said that. Did you run out of insults?

jokes.text: So, so sorry. Cindy, I'm so sorry I'm late. Got held up, but I am ready. What is this? Why did you bring that thing? I told you to get rid of it! Oh, I tried, but apparently I cannot return the doll due to the custom nature of the usage of the doll. Banging its mouth. Right.
jokes.setup: Mac arrives late to the protest plan already in progress.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately translates Mac's 'custom nature of the usage' — 'Banging its mouth. Right.' — confirming everyone knows and cutting through the euphemism instantly.
jokes.explanation: Frank's instant translation is a solid callback payoff. 'Banging its mouth. Right.' from Frank — casual, matter-of-fact, completely unfazed — is good character work. The callback structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Do we serve beer? Because we're a bar.

jokes.text: I don't think so. Stop trying to shoehorn your shirtless-ness into plans that have no need for it. Well, I feel like this is what Dennis would've done.
jokes.setup: Mac is again shirtless in the duster, again trying to incorporate his physique into the plan.
jokes.punchline: Cindy repeats her 'shoehorn your shirtless-ness' line — now a callback — and Mac retreats to the Dennis comparison as justification. The running gag has escalated through the episode.
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the shirtless Mac gag. Diminishing returns are setting in here, though it's still functional. The Dennis comparison as Mac's fallback excuse has been well-established.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I think we just made Paddy's great again.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Shut up, bird.

jokes.text: Cindy's comprehensive, accurate deduction of the orgy: 'I think that you all went to a strip club last night and you got super hammered and horny and the three of you decided to fuck the doll, only to find out that when force is applied to the almost vacuum-tight polyurethane hole, it made a noise. You instantly put it in your mouth...'
jokes.setup: The gang tries to present their doll-tuba idea as a brilliant breakthrough. Cindy asks what she thinks.
jokes.punchline: Cindy's hyper-specific, technically detailed, and completely correct reconstruction of the orgy — including 'vacuum-tight polyurethane hole,' 'you clearly have had sex with the doll multiple times,' and her awareness that this was 'the most insane, disgusting orgy that has ever taken place' — delivered with total calm.
jokes.explanation: One of the two best sustained comedic sequences in the episode. Cindy's calm, clinical, forensically accurate reconstruction of the most disgusting possible night is a masterpiece of comedic writing. 'Vacuum-tight polyurethane hole,' 'clearly have had sex with the doll multiple times,' and 'the most insane, disgusting orgy that has ever taken place' are exceptional choices. The payoff is that she's right about everything, including the detail about Dee sitting back and watching numb. It's a great showcase for Cindy as a character — someone sharp enough to decode the gang's chaos instantly — and a perfect payoff to the entire episode's running threads. Among the episode's very best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So reliable. Yeah, yeah, you can just count on it.

jokes.text: That's dead-on. Yeah, you nailed it. You nailed it. I mean, like... Point by point. You ran home with that one.
jokes.setup: Cindy delivers her devastating reconstruction of the orgy
jokes.punchline: The gang immediately and enthusiastically confirms every detail — no shame, just admiration for her detective work
jokes.explanation: The gang's complete lack of shame — responding to a humiliating accurate accusation with 'you ran home with that one' as a compliment — perfectly captures their moral vacuum. It's also a perfect button to Cindy's speech.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I think we just made Paddy's great again.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Shut up, bird.

jokes.text: And you, Dee, you just sat back and watched the whole thing happen because you are so numb to this kind of behavior that it doesn't even register to you as odd. That's dead-on. Yeah, you nailed it.
jokes.setup: Cindy's reconstruction of the orgy extends to Dee's role.
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately and cheerfully confirms the most damning part of Cindy's assessment — she watched a Dennis-doll orgy and was completely unfazed. The others agree it's accurate.
jokes.explanation: Dee's delighted 'that's dead-on' at being told she watched a sex doll orgy unmoved is a great character beat. The others enthusiastically confirming Cindy's accuracy ('you ran home with that one,' 'point by point') is funny communal complicity.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Hey, Mac, did you gain a little weight?

jokes.text: You can either leave Dennis behind or you can stay the same... playing a doll's asshole with your mouth and talking to something that's never gonna talk back to you. Or will it?
jokes.setup: Cindy is giving the gang a sincere motivational speech about moving on from Dennis.
jokes.punchline: She undermines her own speech with 'Or will it?' — teasing the Dennis return — which immediately triggers the crowd screaming 'Kill it!' when it appears the doll moves.
jokes.explanation: The 'or will it?' as a tease followed by the screaming crowd reaction is a good structural beat that sets up the Dennis return. The pivot from sincere to horror-movie is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Hey, Mac, did you gain a little weight?

jokes.text: Oh. Hey, hey. Take it easy, man. I'm not a doll. I threw that thing on the floor. By the way, what is that thing? I don't like it. Why do you have it?
jokes.setup: The gang thinks the doll has come to life. Everyone is screaming.
jokes.punchline: It's the real Dennis. His first actions: immediately throw the doll on the floor, claim not to know what it is, and demand to know why they have it — while clearly being aware it's a replica of him.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's return is well-executed. His instinct to throw the doll away and his defensive 'I don't like it. Why do you have it?' — while clearly understanding exactly what it is — is perfect character work. Dennis's vanity combined with his discomfort at seeing his own effigy being used this way is rich comedy. The callback to the whole doll arc pays off here.

jokes.text: Mac's shooting his loads into it? Definitely his. He definitely is.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks about the doll. Frank confirms who it belongs to.
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately deduces Mac's relationship with the doll; Frank and the gang confirm without hesitation.
jokes.explanation: Late-episode callback confirming the running gag. Dennis's instant read of the situation and everyone's immediate cheerful confirmation is functional but the gag has been worked hard enough that this is the tail end.

jokes.text: You dress like it's 1998. Your look is played out and so are you. You're basic.
jokes.setup: Dennis dismisses Cindy and tells her she can go now that he's back.
jokes.punchline: Cindy fires back with fashion criticism — 'you dress like it's 1998, your look is played out, you're basic' — sharp but undermined by the fact that she repeats 'basic' moments later when she runs out of insults.
jokes.explanation: Good entry-point for the Dennis/Cindy confrontation. 'You dress like it's 1998' is a sharper line than 'you're basic,' and the subsequent recycling of 'basic' (id 62) is a good structural trap the writers set here.

jokes.text: Screw you guys. Enjoy your crappy lives and your insane, miserable, failed ideas. You guys are played out. You're basic. Uh-oh. Ooh, yeah. You know what? You already said that. Yeah. You did. She said that already. A second ago. Did you run out of insults? Recycling her material.
jokes.setup: Cindy is making her exit with a parting shot.
jokes.punchline: She repeats 'you're basic' — which she already used — and the entire gang immediately points this out in real time. 'Did you run out of insults? Recycling her material.'
jokes.explanation: The trap is well-laid: Cindy used 'basic' once, the audience remembers it, and the gang's real-time fact-checking of her exit speech is a great comedic beat. 'Did you run out of insults? Recycling her material.' from the collective is sharp and fast. The deflation of her power exit is satisfying.

jokes.text: Hey, I don't know about you guys, but I'm a little bit thirsty. Do you guys still serve beer here, or...?
jokes.setup: Cindy has stormed out. The gang is left with Dennis having returned, and there's a slightly awkward moment.
jokes.punchline: Dennis cuts through any potential sentimentality with the most casual possible re-entry — 'I'm a little bit thirsty. Do you guys still serve beer here?' — as if he's returning from a mild errand rather than abandoning his friends for months.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's return after months away being punctuated by a casual 'I'm a little bit thirsty, do you guys serve beer?' is a perfect character moment. The casualness is completely Dennis — no apology, no explanation, no sentimentality. 'Do you guys still serve beer here, or...?' as if he might have forgotten they own a bar is a great final touch. The gang's delight at this ('I knew you were gonna say something funny, man. So smart, too. Clever.') adds to the meta-commentary on how much they missed Dennis's particular comedic energy. High character integration.

jokes.text: I knew you were gonna say something funny, man. So smart, too. Clever. Because we're a bar. Do we serve beer? Funny, man.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks if they still serve beer as if unsure.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's over-enthusiastic reaction to Dennis's mild joke — 'so smart, too. Clever.' — reveals their desperate relief at his return and also functions as meta-commentary: they're celebrating Dennis being funny again after the whole episode was about his absence.
jokes.explanation: This is a callback to the bird joke sequence where the gang tried to explain why Dennis's simple insults were funny — now they're doing the same thing with 'do you serve beer.' The meta layer about Dennis's comedic presence elevates this above a simple reunion beat. Good structural callback.

jokes.text: Well, for now. I'm back for now.
jokes.setup: Mac welcomes Dennis back.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's qualifier — 'for now' — immediately undercuts any sense of resolved reunion. He hasn't committed to staying.
jokes.explanation: Three words that do a lot of work — 'for now' is perfect Dennis. He can't even commit to being back without hedging. The economy is excellent and the character integration is strong.

jokes.text: Guys, you know what? I think we just made Paddy's great again. Shut up, bird.
jokes.setup: Mac celebrates their apparent success with the episode's catchphrase.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's first real action as the returned gang member is to call Dee a bird — immediately, effortlessly, with no setup — and everyone reacts as if order has been restored to the universe.
jokes.explanation: The best single line in the episode and arguably the best-constructed joke. The setup began at timestamp 07:55 when the gang tried to explain why Dennis calling Dee 'bird' was funny even though the word itself wasn't — it was all about the way he said it. For twenty minutes, the gang has been trying to replicate that quality and failing. Then Dennis walks in, Mac says one line, and Dennis drops 'Shut up, bird' — and it's immediately exactly as funny as advertised. The callback structure is flawless: the joke was set up, the expectation was built through absence, and the payoff is exactly what was promised. 'Oh!' 'So reliable' and 'Yeah, yeah, you can just count on it' from the gang are perfect reactions that complete the comedic circle. Economy: three words. Character integration: maximum. This is as close to a perfect sitcom joke as the episode gets.

jokes.text: Oh! Oh! So reliable. Yeah, yeah, you can just count on it. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Dennis just called Dee 'bird' for the first time in the episode.
jokes.punchline: The gang's collective delight — 'So reliable,' 'you can just count on it' — confirms what the whole episode was about: they missed Dennis specifically because of this quality.
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat completing the bird joke trilogy. 'So reliable' and 'you can just count on it' perfectly close the loop opened at the 7:55 mark. The gang's warm reception to something objectively mean as confirmation of restored order is thematically perfect for this show.

jokes.text: Hey, Mac, did you gain a little weight?
jokes.setup: Dennis has just returned. Mac has spent the entire episode flexing his new muscular physique and desperately seeking validation.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's first comment to Mac — with no context, no hesitation — is to ask if he gained weight. All of Mac's work, displayed to everyone who would look, and the one person he was doing it for notices nothing or deliberately trolls him.
jokes.explanation: The perfect closing joke for Mac's season-long subplot in this episode. Mac got massively ripped, failed to find any use for it, was ignored and dismissed by everyone, sought validation from a sex doll — and then Dennis walks in and asks if he gained weight. Seven words. The payoff to the entire episode's Mac thread. It's comparable to the 'Snip snap' anchor example in terms of crystallizing a character's suffering into perfect economy. Dennis either genuinely doesn't notice Mac is ripped (devastating) or is deliberately trolling him (also devastating). Either reading is funny. The music immediately kicks in ('The Boys Are Back in Town'), which makes it even better as a final button.

tmdb_overview: Meet Cindy, the new, ethnically diverse female member of the gang who can successfully pull off scams. Everything is working until Mac introduces a new member: a life-like sex doll that looks exactly like Dennis.
